profiles.title: ETH
profiles.summary: Ethereum’s native asset: settlement, fees and the capital securing the network.
profiles.enables: ETH pays for execution and secures Ethereum through staking. Applications can accept, exchange and use it as collateral without an issuing company promising redemption.
profiles.boundary: D0 describes native ETH at Ethereum’s baseline. An exchange account, staking service, lending position or bridged representation adds its own dependencies.

profiles.title: WETH
profiles.summary: A fixed wrapper that gives ETH a common token interface.
profiles.enables: WETH9 lets applications work with ETH through ERC-20 balances, transfers and approvals. OpenSea documents WETH-funded offers; its Seaport example identifies the canonical Ethereum wrapper.
profiles.boundary: The assessment covers only the recorded Ethereum WETH9 contract. A similarly named token on another chain, an allowance to another contract or the application using WETH needs its own review.

profiles.title: Uniswap v2
profiles.summary: An immutable exchange mechanism that other programs can compose.
profiles.enables: Flash swaps allow a program to receive assets and settle what it owes within one transaction. Uniswap reported $4.8 billion of flash-swap volume from the May 2020 launch through its year-end account.
profiles.boundary: D0 belongs to the reviewed core. The historical activity figure does not establish that every traded token, external wrapper or liquidity position had the same authority assumptions.

profiles.title: Uniswap v3
profiles.summary: A fixed exchange core with concentrated liquidity.
profiles.enables: Liquidity providers can concentrate capital within chosen price ranges. The reviewed core supplies shared exchange infrastructure that applications and interfaces can use.
profiles.boundary: Core immutability does not remove token issuer powers, market exposure or controls in an external position manager. A managed position cannot inherit the core’s D0 automatically.

profiles.title: Uniswap v4
profiles.summary: An immutable exchange core with room for pool-specific logic.
profiles.enables: Hooks let builders add behavior around a common PoolManager. Permissioned Pools documentation illustrates issuer-managed access checks on this open infrastructure.
profiles.boundary: D0 applies to the recorded Ethereum PoolManager. Hooks, tokens and position dependencies remain unresolved unless separately reviewed. The core’s grade is not a blanket grade for every v4 pool.

profiles.title: Morpho Blue
profiles.summary: A reusable lending core with a documented history of adoption.
profiles.enables: Morpho reported more than $1.7 billion deposited on Ethereum six months after launch in 2024. Its later use in Coinbase borrowing shows how a lending mechanism can reach users through familiar distribution.
profiles.boundary: EDI covers the recorded Ethereum L1 core. Market oracles, collateral, vaults and the separate Base deployment are not granted complete D0 coverage by that record.

profiles.title: Seaport 1.6
profiles.summary: A shared settlement mechanism for digital-property markets.
profiles.enables: OpenSea’s documentation identifies Seaport 1.6 for new orders. Its order model connects offers, consideration and settlement; WETH is one asset that can participate in these workflows.
profiles.boundary: D0 belongs to this exact reviewed settlement mechanism. Zones, conduits, NFT contracts and other assets in an order retain their own dependencies.

profiles.title: USDC
profiles.summary: Issuer-backed dollars that participate in programmable settlement.
profiles.enables: Visa’s 2021 Ethereum pilot demonstrated settlement in USDC within an established payments workflow. Dollar-denominated claims can move through onchain systems while institutions remain responsible for issuance and redemption.
profiles.boundary: The issuer and backing remain part of the asset. D9 captures issuer-controlled backing, redemption or seizure; using Ethereum does not remove those powers.

profiles.title: BUIDL
profiles.summary: Institutional fund shares with onchain settlement and liquidity connections.
profiles.enables: BlackRock launched BUIDL on Ethereum in 2024. Securitize’s 2026 UniswapX announcement describes quote-based trading for eligible investors and approved counterparties.
profiles.boundary: Fund ownership, redemption, backing and transfers retain institutional controls. The UniswapX announcement is not evidence of a specific v4 pool or independently measured trading activity.

profiles.title: PAX Gold
profiles.summary: A gold-backed claim connecting a physical asset to token workflows.
profiles.enables: PAXG represents a claim whose usefulness depends on the connection between the token and its gold backing. This profile records that economic role without inventing a current balance or adoption milestone.
profiles.boundary: Custody, backing and redemption remain with the issuer and its arrangements. D9 describes those powers; it does not measure the value of gold or the quality of the custodian.

profiles.title: PayPal USD
profiles.summary: Dollar tokens connected to a familiar payments distribution network.
profiles.enables: PYUSD is another example of issuer-backed money participating in onchain systems. Ethereum activity must be distinguished from activity on other supported networks.
profiles.boundary: The asset retains issuer control over backing and redemption. This profile makes no claim about Ethereum-specific payment volume or customer counts.

profiles.title: Base
profiles.summary: An Ethereum-settled network that extends execution and distribution.
profiles.enables: Coinbase reported more than 2.17 billion USDC in cumulative borrowing originations through Morpho on Base as of 14 April 2026. This is evidence of distribution through an established product, with its chain scope preserved.
profiles.boundary: The October 2026 EDI edition records operator and council authority. The chain assessment is separate from any asset issuer, lending market, oracle or custody arrangement used on Base.

stories.title: Exchange, made reusable
stories.subtitle: A D0 mechanism becomes infrastructure when other programs can use it.

sections.heading: A concrete record of use
sections.body: Uniswap’s 2020 review reported $4.8 billion of v2 flash-swap volume since its launch that May. This is a historical, first-party report of one mechanism’s use—not a current balance or a measure of all Uniswap trading.

sections.heading: Infrastructure that stays available
sections.body: A flash swap lets a program use assets and settle its obligation in one atomic transaction. The lasting contribution is a reusable exchange primitive. EDI’s D0 assessment describes the reviewed core’s authority boundary; it does not claim that decentralization caused the reported adoption.

sections.heading: Follow the actual object
sections.body: Versions v2, v3 and v4 are separate mechanisms. The UNI token, an interface and a managed liquidity position are also separate objects. Their shared name is a useful search term, but cannot supply a shared assessment.

stories.title: A lending core finds new doors
stories.subtitle: An Ethereum milestone and a Base distribution story, with their scopes intact.

sections.heading: First, an Ethereum milestone
sections.body: In August 2024, Morpho reported more than $1.7 billion deposited into Morpho Blue within six months of its Ethereum launch. That dated stock of deposits provides a specific record of use for the L1 lending mechanism.

sections.heading: Then, a distribution connection
sections.body: Coinbase later brought Morpho borrowing into its product on Base. Its April 2026 report cited more than 2.17 billion USDC in cumulative originations as of 14 April. Originations count lending activity over time; they are not outstanding debt and cannot be added to the earlier deposit figure.

sections.heading: The same story spans different boundaries
sections.body: The D0 record covers the exact Ethereum core. It does not grade the Base deployment by association. The October 2026 EDI edition assigns Base a D6 chain assessment, USDC its issuer controls, and each market its collateral, oracle and custody assumptions. Those distinctions make the distribution achievement understandable.

stories.title: The quiet usefulness of WETH
stories.subtitle: A fixed wrapper helps ETH speak the language of token-based applications.

sections.heading: A small interface, widely useful
sections.body: WETH9 wraps native ETH in an ERC-20 interface. Applications can use common balance, approval and transfer operations while a holder retains the wrapper’s fixed route back to ETH. The reviewed Ethereum contract adds no privileged owner to those rules.

sections.heading: A documented connection
sections.body: OpenSea explains how WETH funds offers, and its developer documentation identifies Seaport 1.6 for new orders. Its Seaport example uses the canonical Ethereum WETH address. This establishes an integration and a useful workflow without claiming independently measured trading volume.

sections.heading: Composition preserves distinctions
sections.body: WETH9 and Seaport 1.6 have their own reviewed mechanisms. An order also involves assets, approvals and potentially zones or conduits. A narrow, reliable component is valuable because it can be understood on its own; the entire resulting position still needs its own scope.

stories.title: Dollars meet shared settlement
stories.subtitle: A payments pilot shows what issuer-controlled assets can add to Ethereum.

sections.heading: A historical proof of connection
sections.body: In March 2021, Visa documented settlement in USDC over Ethereum with Crypto.com. The pilot connected a dollar-denominated token to an established payments network’s settlement workflow. It is a specific historical example, not a claim that all Visa settlement moved to Ethereum.

sections.heading: The institution remains part of the asset
sections.body: A dollar token can travel through programmable infrastructure while an issuer maintains its backing and redemption arrangements. EDI’s issuer-control category D9 makes those retained powers visible. That is compatible with a useful contribution to the range of things people can do on Ethereum.

sections.heading: Keep growth correctly attributed
sections.body: Visa’s April 2026 release describes a broader, nine-chain stablecoin settlement effort. Its multichain annualized run rate is not an Ethereum-only observation. This story keeps the well-scoped Ethereum pilot visible and leaves out an unsupported Ethereum growth total.

stories.title: Fund shares gain another connection
stories.subtitle: BUIDL brings institutional claims into onchain settlement and trading workflows.

sections.heading: The asset and its responsibilities
sections.body: BlackRock’s 2024 BUIDL launch put fund shares on Ethereum. The fund’s economic exposure and legal arrangements remain distinct from the token interface. Its issuer, custodian and investor-eligibility controls continue to matter.

sections.heading: A new liquidity route
sections.body: In February 2026, Securitize and Uniswap Labs announced an integration with UniswapX’s request-for-quote system. The described route connects pre-qualified investors with whitelisted counterparties and atomic settlement. This source establishes the announced integration, not an independently reproduced trading-volume record.

sections.heading: Open infrastructure, specific access
sections.body: The opportunity is a useful connection between institutional assets and programmable markets. D9 makes the retained backing and redemption authority legible. UniswapX remains distinct from Uniswap v4: this announcement does not establish a particular BUIDL v4 pool.

stories.title: An open core, different market rules
stories.subtitle: Permissioned Pools illustrate how one substrate can support different access conditions.

sections.heading: The extension point
sections.body: Uniswap v4 separates a shared PoolManager from pool-specific hook logic. Its Permissioned Pools documentation, introduced in July 2026, describes hooks that check whether participants may swap or provide liquidity.

sections.heading: A productive combination
sections.body: An issuer can use open exchange infrastructure while retaining access rules required by its asset or market. The contribution is this ability to connect different assets and participants through a common substrate. High-D components need not promise a future transition to D0 to be useful.

sections.heading: A mechanism illustration
sections.body: EDI’s D0 assessment belongs to the exact reviewed Ethereum PoolManager. This story illustrates documented capabilities; it does not identify a live pool, measure adoption or assign a complete grade to a particular hook. A pool assessment must follow the actual chain, tokens and access-control implementation.

methodology.title: What D measures
methodology.body: The Ethereum Decentralization Index describes additional authority relative to Ethereum L1. D0 means no additional administrator can rewrite the reviewed principal or exit rules. D1–D9 describe forms of additional authority. These are ordinal categories, not probabilities of loss, equal intervals or ratings of economic merit.

methodology.title: Exact mechanisms, separate positions
methodology.body: A brand, token, deployment and user position are different identities. The strongest documented restriction on a relevant dependency path applies. An unresolved dependency prevents a complete assessment; a known floor remains visible. An editorial relationship never changes the EDI dependency graph.

methodology.title: Three independent clocks
methodology.body: The research review date determines assessment freshness. Economic observations retain their own measurement dates and periods. Editorial review has a third date. Nonpermanent research expires on the canonical monthly schedule; permanent D0 mechanisms do not expire solely because of age. Financial updates cannot renew research.

methodology.title: What the stories establish
methodology.body: Stories distinguish a documented capability, announcement, pilot and reported adoption. Historical figures remain historical. Deposits, originations, trading volume and fund assets measure different things. The directory does not total them, infer net external capital inflows or equate activity with value accruing to ETH.

methodology.title: Coverage and corrections
methodology.body: This edition contains 118 canonical EDI records, 12 edited profiles and six stories. Basic records preserve canonical research without inventing adoption evidence. Assessment corrections belong in the upstream EDI repository. Editorial corrections should identify the claim, source and affected object. Original research and source titles remain available in their original language.

collectionDescriptions.d0: Useful mechanisms with no additional administrator over their reviewed rules. Explore exact objects and the evidence of what people build with them.
collectionDescriptions.global-economy: Dollars, fund shares, physical assets and distribution networks participating in Ethereum’s economy—with their actual responsibilities and controls visible.
